zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical review aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0; supplied page subset). Used for lexical cross-checks after reading the BnF scan, not as authority for this copy's spelling, typography, or placement. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Gyokusha is a richly adorned carriage. Queccôna qualifies curuma on the next row; the scan supports n, not the OCR's h, in this adjectival form.
Curuma completes the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese describes a carriage richly ornamented, not a vehicle made literally from a single jewel.
Gyokusen denotes a precious or excellent spring. The headword begins G, and the abbreviated Portuguese Fõte introduces its water.
The water is crystalline, that is, excellent. This short continuation completes the spring entry and preserves the explanatory i, inside the italic gloss.
Gyokuseki is explained by tama no ishi and tama, a precious stone. The following adjective belongs to Portuguese Pedra, not to another headword.
Precioſa completes the precious-stone definition. The short physical line is retained independently.
Gyokusetsu is beautiful snow, with tama used as an embellishing expression. Printed final t in Guiocuxet is retained rather than expanded to a modern syllable.
Ne- plus ue forms neve: very white and beautiful snow. The scan reads muito, correcting OCR maito without modernizing alua or fermoſa.

runs.text: Guiocuxi. Tamano yubi. i, Teiuǒno yubi.

lines.note: Tama no yubi is explicitly identified as the ruler's fingers. The Japanese teiwo phrase supplies the honorific royal reference.
Dedos de Rey confirms that the preceding entry concerns a king's fingers. It is not a separate definition of the following teeth entry.
This homophonous Guiocuxi concerns royal teeth: Japanese fa and Portuguese Dentes agree. It remains separate from the preceding finger entry.
The headword is glossed simply as a star through Japanese hoshi and Portuguese estrela. The initial G corrects OCR C; the entry does not identify a particular astronomical object.
Gyokusho refers here to the sovereign's palm or hand. Teiuǒ- continues with no tanagocoro below; the visible separator after i is a comma.
No tanagocoro completes the royal-hand explanation. Portuguese Mãos de Rey gives hands rather than restricting the gloss to the palm.

This separate gyokusho entry concerns a splendid bed or couch, as yuca and the Portuguese gloss indicate. The damaged middle of the headword is compatible with Guiocuxǒ, not OCR Guincuxǒ; its vowel mark is faint.
Catre supplies the alternative word for a bed or couch. It completes the preceding entry despite occupying only a short row.
Tama no yosowoi denotes splendid appearance or adornment. This is another distinct gyokusho entry, not a continuation of the bed definition.
Ou bello parecer completes the description as a beautiful appearance. The Portuguese confirms the sense of yosowoi rather than a physical jewel.

Tamazzusa and fumi identify a letter or written message. This gyokusho entry develops written-verse senses below. The o and its caron are very lightly inked; the retained Guiocuxǒ is a contextual reading compatible with those traces, not a fully clear impression.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Verſos, ou cantigas eſcritas em hũs

lines.note: The additional sense is verses or songs written on papers. The plural hũs continues into the noun on the next physical line.
The papers are closed or tied together. A second Item begins another usage of the same headword, not a new Japanese entry.

runs.text: Papel com verſos eſcritos honrando a peßoa q̃

lines.note: A paper bearing written verses is named respectfully with regard to the sender. The abbreviated q̃ introduces the relative clause completed below.
The example says that the addressee has bestowed or sent the verses. The scan supports Guiocuxǒuo, correcting OCR Gurocuxǒuo; the attached uo is the object particle.

The translation is 'you sent me some written verses'. The damaged hũs and the congested verſos eſcritos are read with the help of the repeated wording above; the nasal mark and word boundary remain less secure than the surrounding text.

runs.text: Guiocuxocu. Tamano iro. i, Itçucuxij iro.

lines.note: Gyokushoku is a fine or beautiful colour, explained by tama no iro and itsukushii iro. The adjective is not a reference to cruelty despite a tempting modern word resemblance.
Boa and fermoſa describe the colour as good or beautiful. The heavily inked first adjective still supports Boa.
The repeated tama is glossed as precious stones in the plural. The scan supports precioſas, not OCR preciaſas.
This homophonous entry concerns the king's hands, through tama no te. The headword begins G rather than the OCR's C.
Gyokue is a rich garment, explained by tama no koromo. The Portuguese qualification continues below.
E precioſo adds that the garment is precious or costly. It belongs to the preceding clothing entry.
Gyokuei denotes a jewel's shining. Tama cacayaqu is retained as printed; the Portuguese infinitive is divided Reſplan- across the physical line break.
Decer completes resplandecer, and a pedra precioſa supplies the shining precious stone. The verb is not the unrelated descer.
Tama no mushiro is a rich mat. The concise Portuguese gloss confirms the material object without specifying its construction.
Gyokuyo is the ruler's face, explained by tama no kawo. The damaged headword supports Guiocuyǒ; Portuguese Rosto replaces OCR Resto, and the whole Portuguese phrase is italic.
Gyokuza is an elaborately adorned seat or chair. The printed Tamanoza remains joined, and cadei- continues below.
Ra completes cadeira. Ricamente ornada specifies rich ornamentation, finishing the seat definition.
Gyodo here means walking or going in procession. Yuqu michi supplies the Japanese explanation, while mo- continues as modo below.
Do completes modo, yielding 'in the manner of a procession'. The line belongs to the first of two consecutive Guiǒdǒ entries.

This second gyodo denotes throwing out what remains in a drinking cup. Sutçuru governs coto below; a small printed stop, rather than the OCR hyphen, is visible before the right rule. The punctuation is retained despite the syntactic continuation.

runs.text: Vazar, ou botar fora o que fica no

lines.note: Coto closes the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese begins 'empty or throw out what remains', with its location supplied on the next row.
The remainder lies at the bottom of the sakazuki. Sacazzuqui is a Japanese cup-name embedded in a Portuguese explanation.
Gyohai is an honorific cup, belonging to a noble person. The scan reads Guiofai, not OCR Guiufai; the Japanese cup-name also occurs inside the Portuguese gloss.
The example guiofai wo itadaku concerns respectfully receiving or raising the noble person's cup. Its literal gesture is explained by the next Portuguese row.

runs.text: Por na cabeça o Sacazzuqui de peßoa hõrada.

lines.note: The translation describes placing the honoured person's cup on one's head. The second pass distinguishes the printed nasal abbreviation hõrada, with a tilde over o and no n, from the earlier expanded reading honrada. Sacazzuqui is embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
Gyofu is a fisherman, literally a man engaged in fishing. The scan supports Guiofu rather than OCR Gurofu, agreeing with the Japanese explanation and Peſcador.
Gyofuku is the belly or stomach of a fish. The visible f and following u support Guiofucu, not OCR Curoſacu; Vuonofara is retained as one printed string.
Do peixe completes the fish-belly gloss. This is the final body row of the left column, not page furniture.
Gyogaku combines conduct or practice with learning, as Voconai and gacumon indicate. The Portuguese pair 'virtue and letters' continues across this row and the next.
E letras completes the pairing of virtuous conduct and learning. The short line is ordinary body text.

Katachi and kabane explain bodily form or figure. The unmarked Guiogai is retained despite the expected long vowel; the supplied NINJAL index also reports this as a suspected printed anomaly. No final stop or hyphen is secure after esta.
Tua completes Portuguese estatua, followed by 'or body'. The physical division of the word is preserved without supplying a missing hyphen.
Gyogan is a fish's eye, explicitly explained by uwo no manako. Pei- begins the Portuguese peixe continued below.
The example says that fish eyes resemble jewels. The Portuguese translation starts on this row and continues on the next.
The fish's eyes resemble precious stones. The tight printed compedras is retained; the terminal S. is a roman usage label for written language, outside the italic gloss.

runs.text: Guiǒgiǔ. Yuqu. Giǔ ſuru. i, Tachij.

lines.note: Gyoju joins going and remaining, with tachii as an explanation. The enlarged middle Giǔ has a caron above its damaged u rather than the OCR grave; An- begins andar below.
Andar and estar translate going and remaining. The example adds zagua, extending the expression to the customary postures or activities.
The translation continues with walking, remaining, sleeping, and so forth. Item then introduces the broader temporal sense of the expression.
Sempre and em todo tempo give the extended sense 'always' or 'at all times'. This completes the gyoju entry.
Gyogo is an imperial outing, explained by teiwo no miyuki. The final sai- continues as saida in the next row.

runs.text: da del Rey, q̃ ſefaz cõ grande ſolennidade.

lines.note: Da completes saida: the king's departure is conducted with great solemnity. The scan supports da, not OCR du; the abbreviated q̃ and cõ and the tight ſefaz are retained.
This differently marked Guiǒgô refers to deeds or exercises, explained by conduct and action. Its final circumflex must not be copied from the preceding entry's caron.
Cicios completes exercicios. The one-word fragment belongs to the definition of deeds or exercises.

Gyogan here concerns virtuous works performed with an aspiration. The o and its mark in the headword are almost erased but have compatible traces; Guiǒguan is chosen over the OCR's broken Gui guan, with support from the gloss and supplied lexical index.

runs.text: tude que hum faz com deſejo da ſaluação.

lines.note: Vir- plus tude forms virtude. The works are done with a desire for salvation; the long s in deſejo corrects OCR dejejo.

runs.text: Modo de viuer, ou obras. Vt,

lines.note: Gyogi denotes a way of living or one's deeds. The clear headword and its repetition below support Guiǒgui rather than OCR Gurǒgui.
The example describes a person whose conduct is upright or good. Latin l introduces the alternative adjective; there is no printed paragraph sign at the beginning of this row.

runs.text: recto, & virtuoso, ou de boa vida.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the example as an upright, virtuous person of good life. The sense is moral conduct rather than mere outward etiquette.
The distinct Guiôgui is glossed as deception or a lie through itsuwari and Mentira. The circumflex differentiates its printed form from the preceding conduct entry.
Gyogyoshii describes something imposing, exaggerated, or extraordinary. The Japanese obitataxii explanation agrees with the Portuguese continuation.
The Portuguese expands the sense as great, remarkable, or extraordinary. These adjectives complete the preceding headword's definition.
The example applies the adjective to a person who exaggerates or magnifies things. The scan reads fito, 'person', with f rather than OCR long s.
Dor completes encarecedor: someone who makes much of things. This finishes the example rather than introducing another noun entry.
Gyoi here means royal clothing, explained by on koromo. The scan supports coromo and Rey, correcting the OCR's corono and Ry.
The second gyoi denotes the will or command of a noble person. Micocoro supplies the Japanese honorific explanation, and the headword is Guioi rather than Gutoi.
Gyoi ni makasuru means conforming to or leaving matters to the honoured person's will. The Portuguese construction continues with its object below.

runs.text: a vontade, & mandado do ſenhor, ou peſſoa

lines.note: The object is the will and command of a lord or honoured person. The final peſſoa belongs to this same Portuguese sentence.
Honrada completes the preceding phrase. Gyoi shidai means as the lord commands or wishes; the initial h corrects OCR b, and the tilde in mãdar is retained.
The first translation ends with the lord's wishes. A new example begins guioi ni ca-, continued as caqeraruru on the next row.

runs.text: Vir peßoa nobre a minha caſa,

lines.note: Qeraruru completes the Japanese verb. The gloss describes a noble person coming to one's house, with another favour added below.
Giving the speaker something is the alternative favour. A further example, gyoi wo uru, introduces receiving counsel or consulting someone of rank.
The gloss lists receiving advice, communicating, and asking. Its honoured interlocutor is specified on the next row.

runs.text: a algum ſenhor, ou peßoa honrada. ¶

lines.note: The consultation is with a lord or honoured person. The following example evidently concerns gyoi ni iru, but the damaged printed start looks like Guiui-; that u-shaped vowel is retained rather than silently regularized to Guioi-.

runs.text: Estar em graça de algũa peßoa no-

lines.note: Ni iru completes the example of entering a noble person's favour. The Portuguese no- continues as nobre below.
The translation adds pleasing the noble person. A contrasting example then offers guioini or guioi- with a different particle in the continuation.
Uo, not OCR no, completes guioi-uo somuku, the alternative to guioini somuku. Both refer to disobeying the honoured person's command.
The alternative Portuguese gloss is displeasing the lord. This closes the long entry on the honoured person's will.
Gyoja is a practitioner, explained as one who performs religious or virtuous acts. The Portuguese reflexive is ſe, not OCR ſo.
The practitioner exercises himself in virtue or penitence. The verb is exercita, correcting OCR exereita, and completes the relative clause above.
Gyoji is explained by okonai and glossed as offices or ceremonies. This entry is distinct from the administrative-duty sense immediately below.

runs.text: Officio, ou cargo como de procura-

lines.note: The next gyoji is an office, charge, or duty. Procura- continues as procurador on the following row.
The gloss gives the example of a procurator or an office in a community. Guioji- begins the next Japanese phrase; the unmarked o in this occurrence is retained.
The alternatives mean having the duty fall to one, or holding that office. The scan reads gozaru with o, not OCR guzaru; Caber a begins the translation below.

runs.text: alguẽ este officio, ou ter eſte cargo. ¶

lines.note: The translation describes an office falling to someone or being held by him. Gua- begins a further compound continued on the final body row.

runs.text: Officio, ou cargo deſta laya que

lines.note: Gua-chi identifies the monthly duty, and the definition continues on the following page. The printed laya is one word; the separate bottom dura is a catchword, not another body row.
Italic catchword at the foot of the right column. It anticipates the next page and is not counted as a second occurrence in the body text.
